newsitem.title: UK: British "wise man" calls for 1/2 point interest rate cut.
newsitem.headline: British "wise man" calls for 1/2 point interest rate cut.

text.p: A member of the British Treasury's panel of independent forecasters or "wise men," said on Friday that interest rates should be cut to 5.25 percent from 5.75 percent currently.
"I think the economy is still recovering and any rise in interest rates would be premature...I think rates should be cut by half a point to 5.25 percent," Patrick Minford told Reuters.
He also said the pound's recent rally was a result of monetary policy being too tight and he would favour a retreat in sterling's exchange rate to levels seen before its upturn.
The pound has appreciated by 5.8 percent on a trade-weighted basis since early August.
Minford said an easing of monetary policy would pave the way for sterling exchange rates to fall.
His views are contrary to those of fellow "wise man" Tim Congdon who told an evening newspaper earlier he would like to see interest rates rise by 100 basis points.
Congdon, a leading monetarist, was speaking as new figures showed a sharp acceleration in broad money supply. M4 grew 9.8 percent in September compared with 9.5 percent in August.

M4, which comprises notes and coins in circulation, personal and commercial bank deposits and certificates of deposit, has been at or above the 9.0 percent upper limit of the government's official target range for almost a year.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has cut interest rates four times since last December, giving millions of home-owners their lowest mortgage rates for 30 years.
But Bank of England Governor Eddie George opposed the last quarter-point decrease, which took place in June, and has said he would prefer to see rates back up at 6.0 percent.
Both Minford and Congdon are members of the Treasury's panel of independent forecasters which was set up in the wake of sterling's exit from the Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1992.
The panel will submit its next report to Clarke before the November budget.
